editor_spans.body: Derby's naming as the home of Great British Railways is presented as a fresh milestone, but the bigger story is how long the railway has waited for one. The idea of a single guiding body dates back to the post-privatisation fragmentation of the 1990s. Derby won the competition for the headquarters under the previous government. Even so, today's plan has construction starting only in 2027 and finishing in spring 2029.

The scale also deserves a sober look. The building will house up to 450 staff, which matches the 'hundreds of jobs' line, but it is an administrative centre rather than an industrial revival. The more durable asset for the city is the train-building work at Alstom's Derby site, which depends on a steady flow of orders rather than on where managers sit.

The figure that should worry ministers is buried near the end: fewer than 7% of rail workers are under 25. Up to 600 apprentices over four years is welcome, but it is small against an industry whose engineering and driving workforce is ageing out. Public ownership changes who collects the revenue. It does not by itself solve the skills cliff, and that will decide whether 'your train turning up' becomes reliable.

Britain's Ukraine rhetoric has grown steadily louder: 'rock-solid', 'for as long as it takes', 'go further and faster'. The deliverables are steadier and smaller. The headline acceleration is £10 million of a £45 million missile package, set against an existing £1.6 billion multi-year commitment. Meanwhile Ukraine faces its fifth winter of bombardment, and Russia has escalated with jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept.

The energy ceasefire also shows how far the UK's own interests and Kyiv's now overlap. The Prime Minister openly links it to getting diesel back onto world markets, and the government concedes the war's effects on energy prices and household costs. The initiative itself belongs to Washington, with London supporting it and lobbying for it. Russia's escalation after the ceasefire call suggests that pressure through sanctions and LNG shipping bans, slow as it is, matters more than declarations.

The Prime Minister's offer to Holyrood is a former metro mayor exporting the English combined-authority model into a devolved space Westminster does not control. Local government in Scotland is Holyrood's responsibility, so this can only be an invitation. Routed through 'No10 North' and the Scotland Office, it will look to many in Edinburgh like an attempt to build a direct Westminster relationship with Scottish regions over the Scottish Government's head.

The underlying charge, that Holyrood has centralised, has substance after a generation in which services and budgets were pulled towards Edinburgh. But the outcome depends on trust between two governments of different parties. A model announced in a London speech rather than negotiated first is a weak starting point.

The most consequential line of the Commons statement is not the summit date. It is the Prime Minister's call for a 'serious dialogue' about the long-term UK-EU relationship. That is the first explicit opening from a sitting prime minister to revisit the post-2016 settlement. His list of border frictions reads as an itemised audit of what the 2020 trade deal left out: salmon document checks, banned seed potatoes, certificates costing hundreds of pounds per shipment.

The government's estimate of £10 billion a year by 2040 is modest next to the trade lost since Brexit. That gap explains why the conversation is turning to the longer-term relationship. 'The British public will be the boss' is a promise that will be tested if that dialogue goes anywhere. The phrase 'a decade of drift' is the closest Downing Street has come to naming the referendum as its cause.
